newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus parliament likely to approve missile buy.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus parliament likely to approve missile buy.

text.p: Cypriot parliamentarians are likely to approve the island's purchase of Russian-made S-300 missiles in early February as part of their debate on this year's defence budget, an MP said on Monday.

Since the deal was announced earlier this month, Ankara has threatened several times to take military action if the anti-aircraft missiles were sent to Cyprus, where Turkey backs a Turkish Cypriot breakaway state in the north.

"It is expected we shall conclude our debate on the defence budget in the first 10 days of February," said Takis Hadjidemetriou, a member of parliament for the socialist Edek party and chairman of the House Defence Committee.
On Monday committee members met in a closed door session to debate the island's defence budget, which includes a provision for Cyprus's purchase of the missiles.
Cyprus has said the missiles, which it says are defensive, will be deployed 16 months after the deal is approved by parliament.
Asked whether provisions of the defence budget are traditionally approved, Hadjidemetriou answered: "Usually unanimity is achieved."
Turkey pledged on Monday further military backing for Turkish Cypriots on the divided island.

A joint statement released after talks between Turkish President Suleyman Demirel and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash said Turkey and the Turkish Cypriots would establish "a joint military concept" on the island, and that Turkey would build air force and naval bases on Cyprus if Greece continued "entrenching" itself on Cyprus.

Turkey invaded northern Cyprus in 1974 after a coup in the capital Nicosia engineered by the military government ruling in Athens at the time. Since 1993 the Cypriot government has had a defence pact with Greece, its closest ally.
International mediation attempts since 1974 to reunite Cyprus's Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities under a bicommunal umbrella have led nowhere.
